castItem.role: Barry Ussher, a landowner, student, philosopher, &c.
Mrs Grace Tyrrell, (born Desmond), his wife.
Kit, their son, nine years old.
Miles Tyrrell, scholar of Trinity College, Dublin, and brother of Carden.

set.p: The action takes place about the year 1890 in Carden Tyrrell's house on the West coast of Ireland.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Scene:—Carden Tyrrell's library. On the right a door leads to the dining-room and rest of house. On the left is a large empty fire-place. At back through open glass folding-doors a small garden is visible, below which the Atlantic Ocean, flanked by a mountain at left, stretches out to the horizon. Between fire-place and folding-doors stands a writing-table with chairs on either side. At the opposite part of the room near folding-doors is a large sofa. Books in shelves line all walls. In front at the right is another table covered with papers, magazines, &c., which are likewise thrown negligently over other chairs in the room. It is a bright forenoon in the Autumn. Miles Tyrrell, a young light-haired man of about nineteen, dressed in a blue serge suit, is seated at the writing-table in deep study with several books around him. After a pause he looks up wearily, then again bends over his books. Barry Ussher, a lean man of about two and thirty, of medium height, with dark hair, a short pointed beard, and dressed in a riding-costume of sombre grey, enters from garden at back.

sp.speaker: Miles
sp.p: Ah, Barry.

sp.speaker: Ussher
sp.stage: (throwing his hat and hunting-whip on the sofa).
sp.p: Hallo, Miles, good morning. I see you are determined to win that gold medal at Trinity—and become one day Lord Chancellor of Ireland too, I'll be bound.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Lord Chancellor, indeed! I shall be lucky if I can pass my examination and then find just so many briefs as will afford me a living.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Why are you so despondent? You have ability.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Perhaps—if there was an opportunity of displaying it. Oh, this is no place for work.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I know what you mean. But why not study in your room upstairs?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I might do that. Still it is not so much the interruptions. It is the knowledge of what goes on, perpetually.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Are things as bad as ever?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes—my brother and his wife cannot agree.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: How sad it is.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, if only I had a quiet house to study in like yours. You live there like a sage absorbed in your books and ideas.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I fear I also find difficulties in cultivating the tastes that are congenial to me.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You see, Miles, an unfortunate landowner must devote all his attention to keeping a little of his belongings together in these bad times.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: As if you were affected by bad times—you, with that fine place here joining us, and with your unencumbered estate, and no one depending upon you. You're a lucky fellow. No wonder the luck of Barry Ussher is a by-word with the country people.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: They know nothing about it.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Well, in any case you seem able to live as you please. You have always means to travel, and never want for anything.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: So that is your idea of luck, Miles?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Well, somewhat I fancy. Isn't it yours?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I don't think these things make much difference either way.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, come, Barry, you can't expect me to believe that.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes, I mean that what we have on one side is taken away from the other; so the world's lots are more fairly divided than you imagine. Our natures remain much the same at their root. There is always the original pain.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I suppose you cynical philosophers must invent some grievance from lack of real troubles.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: No, Miles.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Well, if you only knew how my brother envies your good fortune.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: There are others Carden Tyrrell might envy, but he need not envy me. By the way, where is he?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: He is out—I suppose in the heather field.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh—
He has finished all his work there, hasn't he?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes, the young grass is coming up beautifully now. Do you want to see him at once? I can send for him. In any case he is sure to be back soon.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: That will do. I am in no great hurry.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You have some business with him?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Well, yes. It is about this very subject of land reclamation. I hear he is about to raise another large loan from Government, in order to extend these operations of his.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: So they told me yesterday in Dublin at the Board of Works.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: When Grace hears this, there will be more troubles and disputes.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Most likely. What a pity your sister-in-law defeats all her objects by her manner towards Carden.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh indeed, she is very impatient with him. Yet she is good enough in her way too.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Precisely; and would probably have made an excellent wife for almost any other man; but for your brother—well, it might have been better if he had never thought of marriage at all.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: What? Surely he might have found some one to suit him. Why should you say such a thing?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes, Barry. But what is the matter with you?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh, nothing, Miles—nothing. I merely meant to say that it would be very difficult for anyone to suit Carden. He is a person so much of himself, you know.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Ah, it is certainly a great misfortune he ever met Grace. And their estrangement is so extraordinary for he once used to be so fond of her.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes, they generally begin that way. I remember just before he became engaged he told me that he thought till then he should never marry, but that at last he had found real happiness. They all say that, you know.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You may very well philosophise over what is past, Barry. But why did you not then try to dissuade him?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Of course I tried to dissuade him then. I did my best.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, you did, did you?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes, of course. I warned him against the danger of marrying a girl with whom he was only acquainted so short a time. I entreated him to wait a while at all events, as he was then only twenty-one and she something younger. But all to no purpose. Ah, if he had waited, he could not have failed to discover that she was only marrying him for his means and position, and that she did not in the least care for him. Besides I was certain from the first that he had no real affection or respect for her.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Indeed? What made you so certain of that, Barry?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Well, you see, Carden and I had been intimate so long. We had been brought up together in fact, so that I fancy I understand him better than anyone. The sudden overturning of all his ideas at that time seemed to me strange and unnatural. He was like one bewitched. A man's whole nature somehow does not change in a moment. You were too young, Miles, to know him in those days; but he was so ideal, so imaginative, as engaging as some beautiful child who saw nothing real in the world outside his own fairy dreams.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I have memories of those days!

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: They are vivid with me. Oh, he always did so fascinate and interest me. What poetry he put into those days of my youth—the days that are dead.

Then to see him suddenly changed, grown even prosy under the power of her influence, it made it impossible for me to consider this attachment of his genuine or likely to endure. And has not the result proved that I was right?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I fear I must admit, Barry, that you were, alas, a reliable prophet.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh, I foresaw all. I knew this change could not last. The old, wild nature had to break out again when the novelty was over. It was a misfortune since he was married, but it was inevitable. There are some dispositions too eerie, too ethereal, too untamable for good, steady, domestic cultivation, and if so domesticated they avenge themselves in after time. Ah, foolishly his wife and her friends thought they were going to change Carden to their model of a young man, but the latent, untamable nature was not to be subdued. Its first sign of revolt against suppression was when he began this vast work in the heather field.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Barry, I—I do not understand.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Miles, you must admit it was rather an extravagant work. He has sunk a fortune of borrowed capital in the reclamation of that mountain. Look at all the men he employed to root up rocks, and the steam ploughs, too, that have been working during these last years.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: But surely he will obtain a large rent for the rich grass he has made to grow there. That ought to more than compensate for his outlay.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Meanwhile interest is accruing. The grass has not grown sufficiently for letting as yet. Then payment of rent cannot follow till long after, always supposing that it ever produces much rent.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Why do you say that? Is not the land good now.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Ah, Miles, do you not know that the soil in such places is very wild and untamable? If heather lands are brought into cultivation for domestic use, they must be watched, they must have generous and loving treatment, else their old wild nature may avenge itself.

div.stage: [He averts his look.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Avenge itself? How, Barry?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Why, the wild heather may break out upon them soon again.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh—
But don't you think Carden has given the best of treatment to the heather field?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I do not know whether his treatment was sufficiently kind, as farmers say here in West Ireland. Somehow he seemed too impatient for the change. He was hardly considerate enough, perhaps, in the accomplishment of his will.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You evidently think there is something unsatisfactory in the business.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Let us hope for the best, Miles. In any case we ought to try and prevent him from embarking in further schemes.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Do, Barry. If there is one person in the world he will listen to, it is you. Besides you will remove a fresh cause of quarrels with Grace: and who knows but you may be able to do more afterwards. Stop—I see him coming now through the garden.

div.stage: [Carden Tyrrell, a rather powerfully built man of one and thirty, with light hair, spare growth of beard, unsteady eyes, very large forehead, and lower part of face small, dressed negligently in a dark suit, enters from the back.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, how goes it with you, Barry? You have not favoured us with visits much of late. What have you been doing?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Well, I have been to Dublin for one thing.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: So I heard. But is it true you are reducing all your rents?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes, I have been reducing them somewhat.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: My goodness. I suppose you will end by making the tenants a present of your property. You call me a dreamer, but it seems that I am the practical man.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh, that does not follow at all. I consider it wiser to give a little in time, than later on to have perhaps more wrung from me by the Land Commission.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: But one should never depreciate the value of one's property. I am afraid, Barry, you are mismanaging your affairs. Have you begun yet to reclaim that bog outside your demesne, as I advised?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: No, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: There, you see. Well, a fortune is to be made by such work. You would be much better employed at it than at reducing your rents. But, my dear old Barry, there is no use in arguing with you, when you are once set upon a thing. I suppose it is because you knew I would not approve of what you are doing that you have not been to see me for so long.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Always suspicious, Carden. But, may I ask why you never come to see me?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You forget all I have undertaken—all my responsibilities. I have little time.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: And one would think my time was of no value. Perhaps, Carden, the real reason is that I might possibly not appreciate some of your undertakings and responsibilities.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Why should you think so?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. I was only wondering.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: But why should that prevent me from going to you?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Precisely, why indeed? I should never have thought of it, if you had not first suggested the thought.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well, you have no reason to think anything of the kind. Just as if I could be occupied in the way you imagine.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: It seems odd that you should, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yet you have an idea all the same, that I could.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Well, to tell you the truth, I heard yesterday that you were contemplating what seems to me certainly most rash.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, you did, did you? Let us hear what seems to you most rash.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: It is true, is it not, that you are about to borrow another large sum of money for new land improvements?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes—it is true—well?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Well—don't you think you had better not?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Don't you think you have done enough work—for the present, at all events? Would it not be better to wait for a time and see whether what you have already accomplished is going to be successful?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes, Carden, don't you think you ought to wait for a while longer?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Wait? Why wait, when I know the work must be successful—nay, is already successful?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You can scarcely yet be sure of that, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Why not?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh, the nature—

div.stage: [He hesitates.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You can scarcely yet be sure of what the land is capable, you know.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Can I not see what grass it has produced.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes, but will that continue?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Will that continue? Who ever heard so absurd a question. As well ask will the air continue to bear up the birds? Will its myriad life continue to pant underneath the sea? Come—my old friend, my brother—I will not have you talk in this discouraging way and make such insinuations, as if you were indeed nothing more than mere country neighbours, who cannot understand my ideas. No, you must believe in me, and inspire me with heart.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: We do believe in you, Carden—but—

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: We only suggest prudence.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Be prudent, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, but when you understand the matter, you will see how prudent I have been. For it was absolutely necessary to obtain this further loan unless the value of the previous one was to be destroyed.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I do not follow you. Will you explain?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well, you see, the drainage of the heather field has practically swamped the lands below it; so I now must necessarily drain the water off from them right down to the sea. When I have finished all that grand ramification of drains, I shall have created a whole vast tract of fertile pasture which will double the value of my property. What do you think of that? Why, I believe all you people imagine that I am working in the dark, that I do not know what I am about. But I tell you I have excellent reasons for everything I undertake.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes, Carden, of course—but you have borrowed a vast sum of money. Take care that the interest you will have to pay the Board of Works does not exceed your income.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: There is no danger, Barry. Have I not told you that my income must be greatly increased?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You have indeed. I can only hope most sincerely that it will be so.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: But you still seem to doubt it all the same.

Oh, come, Barry, this is unfriendly of you. Barry, you are a prophet of evil. Heaven grant that your doubts may be vain, else—Oh, I should be the most miserable of men. But they are vain—they are, they are—even despite your other memorable prophecy that, alas, has come too true. Ah, do you remember your warning to me ten years ago?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You mean just before your marriage? Yes.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I wonder had that anything to do with its unhappiness. I wonder if these doubts now will bring misfortune on my present undertakings.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Carden, for pity's sake stop. Don't speak like that. Forget any doubts I may have now expressed. Forget them—forget them. I was wrong ever to have interfered with my advice. Never will I do so again. No—I have not the right. See, Carden, for all I know you may succeed now. I heartily hope you will. You are determined to, and discouragement might only cause you to fail. No—you must not have a second misfortune to cast at me. Good-bye.

div.stage: [He prepares to go.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, Barry, do not leave us in this way. Think—

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, I am sorry you should take anything I said in that light. I did not mean, Barry, really to—

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: No, Carden, forgive me, but I was for the moment unnerved by the thought that you should attribute to me any of your ill luck. No—I hope you will always find me a help to you instead, whenever you may require me.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, now you are like yourself again—the Barry of other days. I knew you would understand me when I explained everything to you.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I hope, Carden, at least I may never be to you the cause of ill luck.

div.stage: [Exit at back.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Dear old Barry, it makes him positively angry to see me improving my property, because he has not the enterprise to improve his own. But I think I have convinced him that he was mistaken in his estimate of my work.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You certainly frightened him, Carden. I have never seen him as he was just now.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, I really did not mean what I said. He only annoyed me by his stupid doubting.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Still—as a matter of fact long ago he tried to dissuade you from marrying Grace—isn't that so?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes. He was full of doubts and objections then as now—only then he was right. But now—ha, ha— well, I know he is altogether wrong.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Why do you say you know, Carden? Why are you so certain now?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Because I see so clearly before me.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: That at least is a comfort. But perhaps he might be wrong in the other matter too. Don't you think it would be well also if you would determine to belie his doubts of long ago as well as of to-day?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Why, Carden, to try and prove that after all he was wrong when he advised you not to marry Grace.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah—impossible.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Don't say that, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, Miles, you do not understand.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: But have you never tried?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Tried—?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes, tried. You know there is nothing really wrong about her.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Nothing, nothing—and everything. The same thing that is wrong about me. That is how it is between us.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: But might you not try to fall in just a little with her ways? She is good after all.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: My dear Miles you don't know what you are talking about. Of course she is good enough. I know that perfectly well. But she has no sense of compromise —no consideration for me at all. She always despised me.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, Carden, no—

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, but yes. That is why she is so indignant I should take an interest in anything except herself. She would shape my life altogether after her own standard and that of Lady Shrule. I have often given in before, but the result was she became more and more exacting, until at last I found matters quite intolerable. Oh, it is useless to deny that here at least Barry's warnings have come true.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: How extraordinary that you should have changed so towards her—you who once were so devoted.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, Miles, I have simply found her to be absolutely different from what I once imagined her. I was very young then, very inexperienced. I longed for sympathy, and thought it was easy to find. I idealised women in those days. I believed that they were idealists. Ah, that was my fatal error.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: But surely you don't mean to deny that some are?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I don't believe any are, really. They may be on an average more fanciful than man, but your true idealist can only be a man. Alas! had I known that then, my fate would have been very different. I thought others were easy to find, in whom I could confide as in Barry.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Do you consider him an idealist?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I should think so indeed—a true idealist—only he is in a way so drilled and careful, that he will never let himself go. But he is such a friend, and understands everything. No, I never knew isolation when we were together in our youth. Isolation only began with my marriage which led me out into a lonely world. Oh, it was a great misfortune. And I have no one to blame but myself.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: And yet—and yet were you really so much to blame? She was so beautiful—

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, you have said it. There you have found the cause of all the trouble. But Barry would never have wavered.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, he is a hardened philosopher whom no beauty could soften.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: That is because, unlike most people, he can see the truly beautiful, and so is heedless of shams.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Shams? And you can speak like that of her beauty. How I remember her on your wedding-day, when as her little page I held her train? I was only nine years old then, and thought she was some tall white fairy that had come to live with us. Oh, Carden, think of that time. Its memory might banish much bitterness.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Too late, too late. You are still very young, Miles. I have outgrown the capability of such sentiment.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: But you have not outgrown the great kindness of your nature. No, that I could never believe. Ought it not in these difficulties to help you? Why, see how good you are always to me.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, yes, that is different, Miles.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: And Kit, too—are you not most affectionate and kind to him?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: My poor little son, of course—how could I be otherwise to him? He is really so loveable and such a companion to me. For just now he is wonderfully like what you were, Miles, when you acted as that pretty page. His age besides is the same as yours was then; so that the very sight of him calls back to me the days of my youth. Oh, that happy time before my fatal mistake! Miles, do you remember that time?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Remember? How well I remember!

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I suppose I had troubles then, as now; but memory has idealised those past scenes, till only their beauty remains, wafted back to me like an aroma from some lost paradise. I feel I shall never know the joy of those days again.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You must not think such things, Carden. Days as good as these will, I am sure, return.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah no, Miles—their poetry, never—the hope that shines like a spring-day sun upon our youth! It warms us with such life. It inspires us to attempt so many deeds. With what expectations we travel. What materials we are to make out of it all. Do you remember when we went abroad together?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, yes, of course I do, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well, it seems funny that I should have taken you with me then on travels you were too young to appreciate: but I could not bear to leave you who had no protector save me after our father died.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You kind brother.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes, I carried you off, my little Miles, as you were then.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: And how I enjoyed myself.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: What fairie towns we came to—Boppart on the Rhine with its quaint old houses. Then we sailed our boat through the hills to Lorlei, and watched where the river nymphs used long ago to glide, laughing, through the gold-lit depths of the stream.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes, and you told me the legend of their gold— how it was robbed and restored and still guarded by them.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I did; and you, little practical man that you were, you bent down to the water expecting to see the glitter of the Rhine Gold!

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: The marvellous seemed real in those days.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, those bright happy days! And do you remember that Sunday morning in Cologne Cathedral when all the boys sang Palestrina so divinely?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I remember we stood by great iron gates. I looked up in your face and wondered why it shone through its tears.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: How pure the silver voice chords soared to the vaults of stone! Pure as our joy in those days. Fit music for those bright young days.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes, everything seemed joyful then.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, what brave times we used to have together. You know we were always such friends.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Indeed we always were, Carden. There is no one in the whole world I love as well as you. You have ever been the best of brothers to me.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Then you think, Miles, you will always help me?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Why, Carden, of course—

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You will not leave me, if—if ever I should stand helpless and alone, will you Miles?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Good gracious, no. But what makes you imagine such a thing?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well, somehow I feel that persons and objects are receding from me and becoming more unreal in these later times.
sp.stage: (Crosses over to sofa at right and kneeling on it with one knee, gazes out at the mountain.)
sp.p: Do you know, Miles, I often think that my life of pain and unrest here is only a dream after all.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: And like a dream this suffering will pass away, Carden, let us hope never to return.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No, oh no. It would be too much to expect that. A dream—a bad dream
yet with intervals too of wakefulness now and then.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Of wakefulness? What do you mean? When are those intervals?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: When I am out in the heather field.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: The heather field?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes—the great mountain field out there

, that it was my ideal to bring to fruitfulness. There I awaken to true life indeed, as I stand looking over the Atlantic; and sea winds sweep against my feet the young grass in its matchless Irish green that gleams a golden green in the Autumn sun to-day. There I am haunted by those departed joys of my youth—again and again.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: There? But why there, Carden. Why there more than anywhere else?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh you matter-of-fact Miles—still the same as the little wise Miles of long ago, who used to ask such quaint questions. How different we are? Yet how delightful I always find you. “Why there?” you ask. Ha, ha!

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Evidently you consider it a superfluous question. But I think I may very reasonably ask it all the same.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well, then, because there after years of joyless stagnation I find myself again in an ideal domain—away from fretful surroundings—alone! except for little Kit who loves the mountain and its wild flowers. You know, Miles, how like I have said he now looks to what you were in the old days? At moments, indeed, I can hardly believe it is he and not you. So his presence there is no hindrance to that evocation of the past. No; he serves rather to quicken the magic of the heather field.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, to think I could ever have been so much to you. How good you always were to me, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I could not help it. You belonged to the beauty of that time.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: All this sounds like the marvellous tales you used to tell me when I was a child. I see your imagination is the same as ever.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: And you call what I tell you only imagination.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Well, Carden—but what else.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, I suppose I cannot help you. You too are like Barry who said the same thing when I once told him of the voices—

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Voices, Carden? Why— what now are these?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Out there—over the mountain. Oh, the vivid brightness of those voices, as they float back from the past on each changing breeze!

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: You only heard the wind whistle along the coast. Don't heed it any more, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Why should I not heed such celestial song?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: A dream phantom of the desolate mountain.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No; it is only your words I hear as in a troubled dream.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Carden, it is deceiving you—this wonderful imagination.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: What?—imagination again?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Of course.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah well, I cannot convince you, Miles. But what does it matter? You are delightfully sympathetic to me all the same. I feel this opening of my soul to you has even done me good. Yes, it does me good to be listened to occasionally. It leaves a great peace after it; and I have not felt so peaceful as now for many a day. Indeed, if this could last, it would be almost like the old time again.

div.stage: [Mrs Grace Tyrrell, a rather tall, thin woman of about thirty but looking younger, with a pale face, brown hair and an undefinable attractiveness in her outward manner and movements enters by door at R. She is dressed plainly, but with exceeding neatness. Tyrrell takes a large book from the shelves at back of sofa on which he then sits and turns over the leaves, suppressing a look of annoyance.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I suppose you have been out on your rounds this morning as usual, Grace?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes, as usual. Have you been here since breakfast?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Studying, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Not much.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, Barry Ussher was here, and then Carden and I have been talking.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: And so your morning was wasted, Miles?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, not wasted, Grace.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I think it would have been more profitably employed in working for your examinations than in talking to your brother.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I am not at all so certain you are right.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: You must admit you have plenty of time for talking without allowing it to interfere with your studies.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: It is so hard for us, Miles, is it not, when we are together, to refrain?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What you two can have to say perpetually to each other puzzles me. You never visit anywhere nor seem to know what is going on in the neighbourhood.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: If we did, I am certain we shouldn't trouble to speak about it.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, indeed.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No; the subjects that mutually interest us are far different. Among other things, we were talking before you came in over our journey long ago on the Continent.
sp.stage: (Then as if carried away by the subject of the moment)
sp.p: Look, in this architectural book there are plates representing some buildings we saw then. Here is a Romanesque house at Boppart on the Rhine. It is a unique specimen of domestic architecture in that period. And here—this is the bishop's house at Würzburg. How beautifully the oriel is poised there at the angle, like a hooded falcon on its perch; what a genius these medieval architects had for soothing with picturesque ideality the restless suffering spirit of their time. To gaze on their work makes one forget oneself and everything else—

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.stage: (who the while has been looking about her with an impatient and wearied expression).
sp.p: Goodness me, what a litter the room is in with all these books and papers.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What brought me here, by the way, was to tell you that I must have it thoroughly dusted and tidied at once, as the Shrules come to lunch to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes, but what have they got to do with my room?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: We shall want it to sit in. I could not think of letting anyone see it in its present state.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Can't you leave my room alone?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: There! as usual, you are disagreeable when your wife wants anything.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No; but I have a quantity of important papers that it would give me endless trouble at present to sort, and put away.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, why cause him all this inconvenience, Grace? Will not the drawing-room suit you just as well?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Lord Shrule has had an attack of gout and does not like going upstairs—

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Then bring them here. But you need not upset the room. Everyone knows it's a work-room.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I could not think of allowing any strangers to see it in this state.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I wonder how you can attach so much importance—

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: That will do, Miles. As usual you don't know what you are talking about.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Hei-ho.

div.stage: [He begins to gather his books together on the writing-table.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You are not going, Miles, are you?

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I think I shall try if I can read in the summer-house outside.

div.stage: [Exit at back, carrying with him his books.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well, I suppose you had better put away all these old papers at once, and let the housemaid come in.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Impossible.—I am too busy.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: That's what you always say. You imagine yourself the busiest man in the world; and as a matter of fact you have nothing to do.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Nothing to do?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What have you to do?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Very well, we won't discuss that old subject. Anyhow I require my papers, as a man comes to see me to-morrow on business connected with them.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Who is this man?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: The drainage inspector of the Board of Works.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Indeed! Why, I thought he had finished everything here long ago.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, so he has.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well, what is he coming for now?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh—you see—it would take too long to explain just at present. Besides you might not understand.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: You know I would understand well enough. But you never were a person to be relied upon! You are now trying to hide something from me. Come, it is as good to tell it to me at once.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I am not trying to hide anything from you. I don't care whether you know it or not.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well, then, why is this man coming?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: He is to lay out some drains in the valley beneath the heather field.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What?—You don't mean to say you are going to drain all that immense tract of land too?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes. It is necessary now after the other work. So I am going to obtain a new loan from Government to carry it out.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: A new loan! We shall certainly be ruined this time.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No—no—Why, can you not see the enormous improvement this work must be to the estate?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, that is what you are always saying; and the estate for some years past has been steadily growing worse and worse, until now we are almost reduced to difficulties.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You are quite mistaken. I tell you we are on the eve of seeing one income doubled. Just consider the rent that must soon be produced by the heather field.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: The heather field. Up to this, indeed, it has been nothing but a gigantic loss. And who knows but it may never be anything else? My goodness, can you not wait to see if it will be a success before you swamp the estate with this new debt?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No—no—every delay is a loss of profit. You do not understand.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, I am tired of your always telling me that I do not understand. I understand perfectly that you are bringing us to beggary.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well—it is certainly amazing that you should think so. But then, you know, you are never open to reason—never in sympathy with my ideas.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: How on earth can I be, when like everyone else I believe you to be utterly mistaken in what you are doing?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I do not mean what I am doing at present—but the whole tenor of my life and ideas. You have never understood them.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Look here, it's beginning to irritate me this talk about my not understanding. So I see—you think yourself the great incomprehensible, ha, ha. Well, you are quite mistaken. Everyone understands you. So do I, absolutely. For in spite of all your efforts to be singular, you are a very ordinary person, in whom there is nothing particular to understand.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: What on earth do you mean by always harping on my efforts to be singular? Heaven knows I cannot see how I try to be so.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.stage: (with a little laugh, as she taps her foot on the floor).
sp.p: I suppose you are now habituated to the effort.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.stage: (looking at her with a sort of wonder).
sp.p: Oh, how impossible it is for you ever to know how I have suffered —how I have aspired!

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Really, it becomes too provoking when you begin talking about these imaginary sufferings and aspirations of yours. What on earth have you to suffer? You are in good health are you not? Were you not more than fortunate to have married as you did? Have you not independent means? What then can a man like you aspire more to? It is true, of course, that you have crippled your resources by mismanagement and extravagance. But, if you will now be led by me, and put this new scheme of drainage out of your head, and if we are economical for a while, the property must recover. Then you can have absolutely nothing to trouble you.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, this matter-of-fact way you have of looking at things! This simple barren prose of your mind! It is that, that is driving me mad.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Driving you mad—

div.stage: [Pause, during which they look at each other.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Well, I suppose you think I am so.
What an absurd idea. This is another means of annoying me.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I must defend myself.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Seeing you are so bent on ruining our child and me, I can only think one thing.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: That I am mad?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Grace.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well—what is it?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Do you mean this?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What did I say?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You said—I mean you insinuated that—I am mad.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You do not mean this. Take back what you have said.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I cannot.

div.stage: [She still walks to back.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Before you go take back your words. You don't know how they frighten me. Again I beseech you to take back those words. You do not believe what you say.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I do believe them. I believe you to be mad.

div.stage: [Exit at back.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh—ha—mad. How can she say such a thing? Mad—who is saner than I am? Ha—ha—I suppose people of her type think everyone who differs from them, mad. How curious! Ah, we have not a single sympathy. That is what it is.
Merciful heaven, is it possible, though, she may be right? Can there possibly be a doubt as to which is the reality and which is the dream? Oh, horror —horror!

div.stage: [He sinks upon the sofa and covers his face with his hands.
Miles Tyrrell, carrying his books as before, enters at back.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: It is rather chilly reading out of doors. As I saw Grace just go through the garden, I may perhaps again have this place to myself.
Oh, you here still. Why, Carden, what is the matter with you?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.stage: (rising, approaches in a dazed manner, and seems involuntarily to feel his way with his hands).
sp.p: Nothing— only that persons and things now more than ever seem strangely to recede from me and become more unreal. But you—you, Miles, said you would never leave me
if ever I should stand helpless and alone. Oh, Miles, my brother—

div.stage: [He hides his face on Miles' shoulder.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Carden—

div.stage: [The books fall from his arms on the floor.

div.head: Scene
div.stage: Scene:—The same as last, except that the room is tidied, the window doors at back are closed, vases of flowers stand on the tables from which the papers, &c., have been removed and replaced by sundry drawing-room ornaments. It is the afternoon of the following day. Mrs Grace Tyrrell opens the door at right for Lady Shrule, a plain, fashionable-looking woman of about five-and-thirty, in a riding habit and straw hat which fit her to perfection. She enters somewhat jauntily.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I thought we might as well sit here after lunch instead of in the drawing-room. I know Lord Shrule is not very fond of going upstairs.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: No; my husband, dear old man, finds it trying after his attack of gout. Well, upon my word, Grace, this is quite a pretty room. What a pity not to turn all these frowzy books out of it.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, of course, it ought to be a drawing-room.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Then why don't you make it one?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: My goodness, Lilian, you know I can do nothing in this house.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I know you have a wretched time of it, dear, with that husband of yours. Still I cannot help thinking that if, at the beginning, you had really tried, you might have made him more amenable.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: That sounds very easy. You have no idea what he is.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Oh, nonsense, Grace. Most men have notions before they marry: but they are soon brought to their senses, if their wives are clever. And you are clever: so that is why I say you cannot have tried.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I have tried everything, Lilian, although you won't believe it.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What—everything?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: There is one thing I am sure you have never tried.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What is that?

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Flattery.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Lilian, don't be silly. As if there was anything I could flatter him about.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Well, you know, in spite of all, people do say he is clever.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I must say I have never found him so.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I confess I never have either. But then I don't see very much of him. To tell you the truth he always seemed to me odd and ridiculous: for he never cared for society, never went to races, dances, or tennis parties, you know, like other people. Still it might be worth your while to do as I advised. You can hardly imagine what effect it has even on the most unpromising men.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: That may be, that may be, when they are really superior to one; but to flatter him—ugh—never
sp.stage: (half to herself as she turns away).
sp.p: Besides it is impossible after yesterday.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Yesterday? What happened yesterday, Grace?

div.stage: Grace is silent.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What is the matter, dear?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, nothing, Lilian. I did not mean you to hear.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Oh, but there is something, Grace. I see it by your troubled look. He must have done something dreadful yesterday. Perhaps I might be of help to you. What was it?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well this. Yesterday I discovered that he has embarked on a new folly which must end in our ruin; and when I tried to remonstrate with him he would not listen to a word I said.—Just think, he—he—

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: He must be a great savage. But what else can you expect from the life he leads?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Quite true. You are perfectly right, Lilian.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What is this new folly you say he has embarked on, Grace?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, a monstrous plan of draining another immense morass. As if our means were not already sufficiently crippled by his extravagance in this way.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I should think so, indeed. What a misfortune for you that you ever married him.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes—what a misfortune!

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I have always wondered why you did, Grace. You know you never cared for him. How, indeed, could any girl care for such a man—least of all the Grace Desmond I remember in those days, when we used to meet at every party and ball in the county.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes, yes, Lilian, I know that. But you see he was a good match at the time; and I thought I would be able to make him sensible, and to lead him;—for he was so much in love with me.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Was he ever really, do you think?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, I think so: he must have been at first; for then it seemed to me that I used to monopolise all his attention.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: How came he to change? Some other woman, I suppose—

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: No—no. There is no one else. I am sure of that. I have watched him closely now for some years.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Nonsense, dear—just as if you could watch him. I tell you it is impossible that a man can exist without loving some woman.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes—I know we women all think so. But this is quite a case in itself. He is such a queer creature. You cannot imagine how strange his ideas are.
Oh, no—there is no one else; and it is very wicked of you, Lilian, to suggest such a thing.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: How then, do you account for his behaviour?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I cannot think, for I have always been most amiable to him and patient with his eccentricities, which are dreadfully irritating. Gracious, I remember when he first began to weary me with his strange ideas that I could not make head or tail of. (So you may be sure, dear, they were sheer nonsense.) It was then, when I tried to draw him from such folly, and to centre his interest upon myself, that I noticed a curious change in him. It seemed all at once that I became as nothing to him—that what he loved was something mysterious— beyond me.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Ah, he never loved you, Grace. I am certain, now, he never did.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, yes, he must have at first. You should have seen how I made him do almost anything for me. Why, he settled down, entertained, shot, even farmed. Imagine that for him.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Well—what was the result? What about the farming, for instance?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Indeed—the only result of the farming has been—the heather field.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Ah, Grace, for all you made him do, you were not able to make him give up the heather field—my poor Grace!

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, that folly! That abominable work! With the beginning of it I noticed his first change towards me.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: He never loved you, Grace. He is a terrible man. These Tyrrells were always a queer lot. You know the father was very eccentric; and the mother— well, Shrule tells me she went quite out of her mind before she died, at the birth of the young brother. What kind is he, by the way? He is very good-looking, don't you think?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, Miles is all right. He is a harmless creature, —wonderfully clever at college, I hear. He is certainly amiable, but vexes me occasionally with his foolish admiration for my husband.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Yes, I can imagine how annoying that must be.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes, and to have that fellow Ussher, too, dropping in to complete the mutual admiration society! Oh, I always disliked him.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I don't think much of him either, with his sad, lonely way of living there in that great place of his. I believe he has it filled with such strange things.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes, books and hideous pictures. I have not been there for years. I avoid him as much as possible; for he was always my enemy, and does his best to destroy whatever influence I might have with my husband.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: My poor Grace, what a strange crew you have fallen among! This dreadful husband! So at last he is going selfishly to sacrifice you for the gratification of his theories and whims.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: He shall not sacrifice me, Lilian. I am certain of that now.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Why, dear, what are you thinking of?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: All those facts you have mentioned about the Tyrrells only confirm a suspicion that has haunted me for some time.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What suspicion, Grace?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: That my husband is not in his right senses.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Do you mean you think him mad?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes—mad.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes, Lilian; I feel there can be no doubt about it now. You know his monstrous extravagance, his wild manner of talking—and then what you tell me about his father and mother.—Oh, he must certainly be mad.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I suppose you are right.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Of course—that is what it is—poor man! Measures ought therefore to be taken at once to prevent him from ruining his family.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What measures can you take, Grace?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I don't see why I should not commence a legal suit to deprive him of control over the property.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: But that would mean placing him under restraint, wouldn't it?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I suppose so, if necessary. All I know is that I am determined to prevent this new burden from being put on the estate.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Wouldn't it be well, Grace, if you were first to have medical advice as to the state of your husband's mind?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I have already thought of that, Lilian. I have been in communication with Doctor Dowling and Doctor Roche.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What—really?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes. I believe two doctors are required, are they not, in cases of this sort?

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: I don't know: but we can ask Shrule.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Of course: he is sure to know. How lucky I have you both here.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: When do you think of sending for the doctors?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well, Lilian, the sooner the better, if this government loan is to be stopped.
Well, the fact is I—I have sent for them to-day.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: To-day?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes. Was I not right?

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: But your husband suspects nothing of this?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Good heavens, no! Neither do the doctors as yet. No—I have sent for them upon the plea of their holding a consultation about Kit. As Doctor Roche has been attending him lately off and on for little attacks of feverishness and nausea, their visit will not look in any way suspicious. I will then take care they have conversation with my husband. You see?

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: What energy and resource you have, dear, to be sure.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Ah, when a woman is reduced to such desperate straits as I am at present, it sharpens her wits. But the doctors may arrive now at any moment, and as I must see and prepare them beforehand for this task, let us go out to the end of the shrubbery where we can meet them on their way.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Very well—and you can bring Shrule to join in our consultation afterwards, when he comes from the dining-room.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: What a comfort, Lilian, to have you both to consult.
You must help me. I tell you I must succeed in this undertaking. It means the very existence of my child and me.

div.stage: Carden Tyrrell enters hastily at the back.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, have you finished lunch so soon? How do you do, Lady Shrule?
I hope you will excuse my absence. I was very busy all the morning with the Board of Works inspector.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Oh, not at all. Have you finished your business?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No—but I expect to by to-night. The inspector has gone in before me to lunch—so, with your permission, I will leave you to look after him.

sp.speaker: Lady S.
sp.p: Of course, Mr Tyrrell—we will excuse you. Grace and I were just about to take a stroll around the garden. You will find Shrule in the dining-room.

div.stage: [Exeunt Lady Shrule and Mrs Grace Tyrrell at back. Carden Tyrrell gazes after them as they disappear in the garden, then goes to writing table where he searches for something which he cannot find, while he grumbles indistinctly. He looks around the room with an expression of annoyance at its altered condition, then exit by door at right.

Enter at back Barry Ussher and Kit Tyrrell, a rather wild though pensive-looking boy with short, fair hair, and dressed in a sailor suit. He has a daisy chain swung across his shoulder, and holds a bunch of wild flowers in his hand.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Come in, Barry, come in. I missed you yesterday. Have you brought me anything this time?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I am afraid nothing this time, Kit. You see, when I left home I did not intend to come here; but on the road I met by chance Doctor Roche, who told me he had been sent for by your mother. So I thought I would just turn in, and see if anything was the matter. There is no one ill, is there?

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: No, of course not. They are only bringing him to bother me again. I have nothing the matter with me; and still he is always saying I must not eat this and I must not eat that.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: What a nasty old fellow!

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Yes—isn't he horrid? He says, too, I mustn't lie on the grass. I suppose he'll soon want to prevent me hunting for wild flowers.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: That would be a privation, Kit. You love them so much, don't you? What nice ones you have brought in to-day. Where did you get them—so late, too, in the year?

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Oh, you can't think how I had to search for them here and there through the long grass in the heather field. It is the only place now where any wild flowers are left. How I love being there with father.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: So you, Kit, have also caught the sickness of the heather field.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: What is this sickness you are all saying I have? I tell you I am quite well.
Oh, how I wish I were a man.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Alas, are you not much better as you are? Why do you want to be a man?

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Because then they could not prevent me doing what I like. I should be a sailor and find out what is beyond that great sea father and I are always looking at from the heather field.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Be a sailor, Kit, and give up the wild flowers?

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Oh, I forgot. But should I have to, do you think?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I fear you could not gather flowers on the sea, except, perhaps, a few poor crushed ones, torn from its depths by the storms.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Then there are some, after all?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes—down under the sea grow numberless fair flowers whose leaves close softly around many a poor sailor.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: What beautiful flowers!

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I hope you will never be such a sailor, Kit. No, you are far better as you are! Do not wish to be a man.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Why, Barry?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Because you understand so many things now you never could then. How much nicer to be always a little wildflower elf! In the lives of dream children such as you it is beautiful to think of a heather field.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Oh, but can they prevent me from going there?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: They cannot. I will see that old Roche attempts no such tyranny.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Oh, thank you, Barry. How good you always are!

div.stage: Lord Shrule, an elderly benevolent-looking man dressed in a somewhat old-fashioned riding costume, Miles Tyrrell, and Carden Tyrrell enter by the door at right.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: Now that the inspector has gone out again to his work, I must say, my dear Carden, I am astounded at hearing of this new expenditure you contemplate. I did not like to speak before him—Ah, Ussher, how do you do?
And how is my little man?

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Very well, thanks.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: That's right, that's right. I was saying, my dear Carden, your fresh project of expenditure fills me with amazement. Have you heard about it, Ussher?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I have indeed.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: Well, does it not seem to you extremely imprudent—nay, reckless?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Oh, you must not ask me, Lord Shrule. Carden seems determined. And, after all, he is the best judge of his own affairs.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes, Barry, that is just it.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: Come, come, Carden, you will not mind the advice of an old man who has a long experience in the management of land. Your father and I were always fast friends, and I naturally take a great interest in you and your family.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I know you have always been very kind, Lord Shrule. Forgive me if I have spoken hastily. I did not mean—

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: Of course not, my dear Carden. I quite understand you. I fear indeed you must think it rather impertinent of your friends to interfere in your business. But then, as I have said, I consider myself privileged.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You may be quite sure, Lord Shrule, I could not take anything from you except in good part.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: I thought so. Well, let me implore of you, if only for the sake of your family, to desist. This is certainly the wildest scheme I ever heard of, and couldn't pay, even if the drainage were to turn out a success.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: But you forget it is necessary now that the drainage of the heather field falls into this land. I must make a cutting for the water to get to the sea. And then, what is easier than to reclaim the land through which this cutting goes?

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: My dear Carden, don't mind the cutting— don't mind the heather field. What you have only got to think of is to cease altogether from loading your estate with an ever-growing burden of debt. For goodness' sake leave these works alone. If you continue them you will simply beggar yourself.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I do not see that at all. The work will be very remunerative. It will double the value of the estate.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: Oh, Carden, listen to me. I know well the nature of such works as you are carrying on. I have tried them myself—on a far smaller scale, of course. They never repay their expenditure.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: That is a mere assertion unsupported by argument. On the other hand, I have excellent reasons why I should believe that what I am about to undertake must have the best results. Look at the rich pasture now in the heather field. And am I to suppose that I shall not have the same in the valley when it is reclaimed? Until you can prove logically that I am mistaken, I must continue those works, which I clearly see are so profitable. Am I not right, Barry?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I have said I shall never again discourage you, Carden.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: Ussher, upon my word I thought you knew better. But I suppose it is useless remonstrating on these experiments, which amount with him to absolute mania.

div.stage: Mrs Grace Tyrrell enters at back.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, Lord Shrule, we have been waiting for you in the garden. Won't you come? I want to show you my little greenhouse. The plants you gave me are doing so well in it.

sp.speaker: Lord S.
sp.p: I am delighted to hear you say so, Mrs Tyrrell. Let us go and see them. But I hope you will not make me walk much, as I have barely recovered from that last attack of gout, and can only get about as yet quietly on my pony. Let me see, I left my hat in the hall.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: We can go through there, just as well.

div.stage: [Exeunt Lord Shrule and Mrs Grace Tyrrell by door at right.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: It is really too bad that I should be molested thus perpetually with unsolicited advice. All my acquaintances seem to consider it incumbent upon them to interfere in and direct my affairs just like their own. One would think I had no right to do anything. That old fellow, you know, means well; but it is very annoying to be taken to task by a person who has really no right to meddle. Ha!—it is too absurd indeed that I should have to defend what I have a perfect right to do.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: I know it must be very trying, Carden.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I should think so, indeed. And I am not going to stand it any longer. I will live my life as I want, and will take dictation from nobody.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: But you must expect to be criticised, Carden. That is the penalty, you know, for attempting to do anything.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, I don't mind any amount of outside criticism —nor even the strictures of friends like Lord Shrule, as long as their remarks are not to my face. No, it is other criticism—nearer that leaves a sting.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Well, Carden, I am sure Barry and I are not in the habit of finding fault with you. At least we never mean to.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Of that, at all events, I am certain.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No—not you two, kindest and best. It is even nearer home—this criticism and opposition—this hearing perpetually amidst the strain of labour, bitter and disheartening words. That is what is so unbearable.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Be patient with her, Carden. Grace cannot as yet understand. This is a period of trial. One day you will see her loyally helping and inspiring you.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Inspiring me! I wish, Miles, you would not use a sublime word in a vulgar sense. When you have more experience you will find that instead of inspiring they more often prevent us from doing anything.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Oh, Carden—how unlike you! That is more the style of the cynic philosopher, there—Barry. See how he is smiling. I am sure he regrets he missed saying such a thing himself instead.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Well, really, Miles—

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, you dear Miles. You were always the most wonderful body in the world for dispelling bitterness and gloom with that beautiful light you seem to carry about you!

Well, two friends such as you ought to compensate me for what I have to bear from others. Bah, I will not mind them. I will be merry while I work; and my work will be incessant, leaving no time for brooding over unpleasant things. And both of you will always be present with me, if difficulties should arise. Yes, with you I know I cannot suffer defeat from the rest.

div.stage: Enter at back Mrs Grace Tyrrell, Doctor Dowling, a thick-set man of about forty, dressed in a tweed suit, and Doctor Roche, an elderly, lean and somewhat prim man, wearing spectacles and black clothes. Looking a little ill at ease, the Doctors exchange salutations with Tyrrell, Miles, Ussher, and Kit.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Mother!

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Yes, my dear?

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Who is that with Doctor Roche?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Doctor Dowling.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Is he coming to see me too?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Just to look at you, Kit. That's all.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: But I have nothing the matter with me, mother.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Never mind—neither will hurt you—only save you from possible peril—oh, my own sweet boy.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: You cannot think there was cause for summoning these two physicians.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Cause?—well—I was a little anxious on the child's account, and thought it best they should consult about him. But I expected to find you alone.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Carden, I must go. I hope there is nothing really the matter with Kit. He doesn't look as if there was.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Oh, Barry, don't go. You know you promised—

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Hush, Kit.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes, stay where you are, Barry. There is no reason for making such a mystery of this business. Besides, I must soon go out to the inspector, and we can walk together.
By the way, what has become of the Shrules?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, Lord Shrule had to return home suddenly about some matter of importance. They both desired me to say “good-bye” to you.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: So much the better.—Well, doctors, I certainly cannot understand the necessity of this consultation. The boy seems to me perfectly well.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: No, I assure you, Doctor Dowling, he is not so. He is often ill from eating all sorts of unwholesome sweets. How do you find him looking to-day, Doctor Roche?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: He appears healthier, on the whole, I think, Mrs Tyrrell.
Come here, and let me look well at you, my little man. There, put out your tongue.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Ah, I suppose, Barry, I must now expect the worst.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Never fear, Kit. They don't look as if they meant to do much to you.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I am afraid, Mr Ussher, you spoil him as much as his father, and I shall get no good of him while you are here. You and Miles ought to take a walk. It would be so nice on this fine day, wouldn't it? But won't you return to dinner? Do return to dinner, Mr Ussher.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: No, thank you, Mrs Tyrrell, I regret I cannot. I shall be going now in a minute with Carden. Kit must not expect any countenance from me.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: But I thought you said you would not let Doctor Roche—

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Now, Kit, you must do as you are told. Have I not said you needn't fear?

div.stage: [The Doctors look at Kit, feel his pulse, talk together, &c.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Your sister-in-law seems particularly anxious to get rid of us.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.stage: (aside to Ussher, with an enquiring look).
sp.p: Do you really think so? I wonder why?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I am not certain yet.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: How needless this consultation is, to be sure. There is nothing the matter with the boy.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: You do well to say so—you, who are the chief cause of his illness.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I, the cause?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Of course you are. He is sick at night after those long days when you keep him out fasting on the mountain, and then feed him with sweets at dinner afterwards. This must all cease.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Oh, mother, do not prevent me from going to the heather field. I don't want these sweets—I was only sick once.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Can you not see, Kit, that I am only acting for your good?
It is I who fight for his interests, and he leaves me for his father.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Only sick once, and all this fuss for that! Never mind, Kit, you shall not be prevented. I will take care in future that you get plenty to eat and at proper times. So there will be no danger of sickness again.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Then you will not let anyone prevent me from going with you, father?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ah, you see, Kit, I never could get on without you in the heather field. We should feel so lonely—both of us, shouldn't we?

div.stage: [Grace looks significantly at the Doctors, who now begin to observe Tyrrell closely.

sp.speaker: Kit.
sp.p: Yes, father, dear.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: The doctors seem strangely inattentive now to Kit and his ailments.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.stage: (aside to Ussher, with a puzzled expression).
sp.p: So it seems. What do you think they mean?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Wait. I have an uncomfortable suspicion. It is well we stayed here.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Alas, the child's health must be sacrificed like everything else, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: How sacrificed?

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Oh, to add zest to your infatuation for that mountain.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Nothing of the kind. If I had known he had ever been ill, I would have taken every precaution, in spite of my infatuation as you choose to call the interest I take in my work.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Is that your land work, Mr Tyrrell?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: You are an extensive reclaimer of waste land?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes; I fancy there are few in Ireland more extensive.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: You are certainly most enterprising.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Ay—it is a grand work.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: And you believe in the possibility of its paying?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Of course. Wait till you see the profits I shall make. With these I shall extend my works; and with the further profits I shall embark on such a scale of business as in time will enable me to start a company for buying up and reclaiming or reafforesting every inch of waste land in Ireland.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: That is truly a gigantic scheme, Carden. Look here, I must really be going; and your inspector, too, must be waiting for you. Let us be off. Come along.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, wait a moment, Barry. I want to explain. I will go with you directly.

With the far-reaching usefulness of my projects I must become a real benefactor to the country, and in a time, too, when so many quack remedies in the way of legislation are being offered to the public.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: True, true. How very interesting.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Upon my word, most interesting.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Oh, the work is a glorious one. There is something creative about it—this changing the face of a whole country! None of the humdrum, barn-door work of ordinary farming, with its sordid accompaniment of the cattle fair! When from the ideal world of my books those people forced me to such a business, I was bound to find the extreme of its idealisation.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: What the dickens does he mean by that?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: You mean you have idealised farming, Mr Tyrrell?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Of course, what else? Do you think I could go on doing the dull drudgery they forced upon me? No— I considered how I could elevate it. I pondered and pondered and never rested, until at last there came to me the master-thought of the heather-field.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: Oh,—indeed. Dear me.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.stage: (with evident pleasure at the surprise he is creating).
sp.p: Yes; was it not a discovery? And what contentment it brought after the previous life-drudgery. I felt like returning to my youth's ideals in that free mountain air. Oh! there is magic in those mountain breezes!

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: All I know, sir, is, that the Faculty consider sea air blowing over a mountain bog to be the finest remedy in the world for bile or dyspepsia.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: So that is the only thought suggested to you by the ethereal mountain breeze! There are some people who can never recognize a beautiful meaning in anything.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Maybe so, Mr. Tyrrell.
Do you find any meaning yourself, though, in this mountain air?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Do I? Why, of course I do. I find in it a medium between the beauty of the past and myself.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Indeed.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes; nature's ethereal phonograph, as it might be, treasuring for my delight past ecstasies of sound. I hear in its waves those voices floating back to me from—

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You must take your brother away at once.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: What is that you are saying, Mr Tyrrell?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: Voices—you don't mean to say you hear voices?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: I do mean to say it.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Whose voices do you hear?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Choristers singing of youth in an eternal sunrise!

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: But you must know that this is all imagination.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Imagination—always imagination. How wearisome that word sounds to me. I tell you there is no such thing as imagination.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: That is a bold statement, sir.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No—you either perceive or you don't perceive. Therefore it vexes me, when I perceive anything, to be told that it is only imagination.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Wouldn't it be more accurate, then, to call it hallucination?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: That's always how you enter into the spirit of my ideas.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: You can hardly expect her to agree with them.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: No—I suppose there must always be distortion of my meaning.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Then would you mind explaining your meaning?

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: You told us you hear voices?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes, of course.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: Do you ever remember anything they say?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Well, would you let us know?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: They keep telling me I am not what I am.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: How very strange!

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: Humph! do they say anything else, sir?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: They often call me back to my real life.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: What do you mean by your real life?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: That life before I wandered into this dream.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: And so you think you are only dreaming now?

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: How can you tell that you also are not now in a dream?

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Answer that, if you are able, doctor.

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: A man ought to know very well whether he is asleep or awake.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: That is just it; and I know I am in a dream.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Really, Carden, I don't see what you gain by discussing your ideas with people who can neither understand nor sympathize with them. Come, come away. I cannot wait any longer.

sp.speaker: Tyr.
sp.p: Yes, Barry, I suppose you are right. It was stupid of me. Let us go out. Good evening, doctors.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You walk on with Miles and Kit. I just remember I have something to consult Doctor Roche about.

sp.speaker: Mil.
sp.p: Come, Carden.

div.stage: [Exeunt at back Carden, Miles, and Kit Tyrrell.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Doctor Dowling and Doctor Roche, you were sent for by Mrs Tyrrell to-day to consult on a matter altogether different from the health of the little boy.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well, then, and if they were!

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Your husband fortunately suspects nothing; and I have warned Miles against saying anything to enlighten him.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: If you consider me in your power, you are greatly mistaken.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: I consider nothing of the sort, Mrs Tyrrell. You have strangely misunderstood me.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: I don't know. Anyhow, I have nothing to fear from you. The opinions of Doctor Dowling and Doctor Roche will ensure the success of the measures I have decided upon for the security of the child's interests and mine.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: You seem very sure as to the conclusions these gentlemen are to arrive at.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Well, they know all about my poor husband's reckless expenditure, his inability to act like other people, his futile disputes with the tenantry, and to-day they have seen how he has conducted himself, and have heard him speak. I hardly think they can have any doubt as to the condition of his mind. What do you say, Doctor Dowling and Doctor Roche?

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: I am of opinion, ma'am, it is a case of dementia —but curable with proper treatment.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Indeed. And what are your reasons for considering it dementia?

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: The general tenor, Mr. Ussher, of the patient's behaviour; his reckless expenditure of his means, as Mrs Tyrrell says; his queer deranged enthusiasm; and, above all, his talk about hearing voices. There is no more common sign of insanity than for persons to believe that they hear voices.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: Quite so. That is by far the most serious symptom in the case.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: But surely you must see that a highly-gifted man like Carden Tyrrell is not to be judged by your everyday rules. These voices you speak of he heard long ago in happier days. They are only memories made vivid by the force of imagination. Why, he told you as much. Did he not?

sp.speaker: Dow.
sp.p: That was not the impression conveyed to me.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Doctor Roche, you cannot agree with this, I am sure.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: Well, really, Mr Ussher, I fear I must—that is to say, with certain reservations. Our responsibility in certifying to madness is no doubt grave; but then, on the other hand, we would incur a graver responsibility if, by our indulgence, the patient afterwards were to harm himself or anyone else.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: If he is not restrained he will surely bring the child and me to irreparable ruin. You see he has almost done so already. Oh, think of that, Doctor Roche. You know he is not fit to have the control of anything.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: I know there might be some doubt as to the question of madness, if we had nothing more to go upon than these extravagant land improvements of his.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: But then I am confronted by this unpleasant symptom of his hearing voices that have no existence— a most common sign, as you say rightly, Dowling, of insanity.

sp.speaker: Uss.
sp.p: Did not Joan of Arc declare she heard voices calling on her to accomplish a work which proved to be one of the most wonderful and practical in history? Was not Socrates firmly convinced that he was in the habit of receiving admonitions from his dæmon? I might quote you several other instances of celebrated personages whose imaginations led them to believe they heard voices. Yet no one has ever thought of calling them insane. Come now, Doctor Roche, a man of your experience and culture must admit the truth of what I say.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: Ah, Mr Ussher, I fear all forms of madness might be explained away by your arguments.

sp.speaker: Gr.
sp.p: Of course, Doctor Roche. Pray don't listen to him.

sp.speaker: Roc.
sp.p: But, at the same time, Mrs Tyrrell, I am bound to admit that madness partakes more of an infirmity whereby the natural sequence of ideas is disconnected.

sp.speaker: Uss.
